Historical Perspective ♦ 7
अमूर्तं यजमानस्य ह्यभावे च विनश्यति ।
अच्छिन्नं शाश्वतं नित्यं प्रतिमाराधनं परम्।।
(यज्ञाधिकारे, १, १०-११)
Sacrificial rituals (like agniṣṭoma) will be effective only during the lifetime of the performer of those rituals (agnihotri), and their rewards are confined to the performer and his immediate family. But the temple constructed or an icon installed will bestow benefits not only on the donor and the priest but on all the people who visit the temple and worship the icon. Further, every sacrifice has its own specific reward to confer upon. The performer and it is incapable of occasioning other benefits. Iconic worship in a temple, however, will fulfil all the desires of the devotees (sarva-kāma-prada), and it is capable of bestowing the benefits of all the sacrifices (sarva-kratuphala-prada), (ibid, 1st patala)
स्थापितां प्रतिमां विष्णोः सम्यकसंपूज्य मानवः ।
यं यं कामयते कामं तं तमाप्नोत्यसंशयम्।।
यथा हि ज्वलनो वह्निस्तमोहानिं तदर्थिनाम्।
शीतहानिं तदन्येषां स्वेदं स्वेदाभिलाषिणाम् ॥
करोति क्षुधितानां च भोज्यं पाकक्रियां शिखी।
तथैव कामान् भूतेशः स ददाति यथेप्सितम्।।
कल्पद्रुमादिव हरेर्यदिष्टं तदवाप्यते ॥
(प्रकीर्णाधिकारे ३५, २३-२९)

particular place and protected from conditions of its disappearance was the symbolic significance of the main and immoveable icon in the sanctum (dhruva-bera). The “āhavanīyāgni” which is lit from the 'gārhapatyāgni' and taken out and used for daily rituals is like the moveable and representative icon for which any routine worship is offered (kautuka- bera for nityārcanā): and another fire, known as 'dakṣiṇāgni' corresponds with the third icon (processional, autsava- bera) which receives special and occasional worship (viśeṣārcanā). This is how the sacrificial cult was transformed into the cult of iconic worship: the 'fire-triad' (tretāgni) became the 'icon-triad' (bimba-traya).
The ground was now prepared for the development of a full-fledged temple-culture and a new slant was given to the Vedic idea of sacrifice (yajña) when iconic worship also was accepted as a yajña. The details of a yajña of the old type were woven into the fabric of worship in a temple. The daily tending of the household-fire (agni-hotra-paricaryā) was now substituted by daily worship in the temple. Special worship during the five special occasions (pañcaparvārcanā), and during the four rainy months (cāturmāsyārcanā) were the new versions of the old ‘darśa-pūrṇa-māsa' and Āgrayaṇa. If Soma-yāga was the annual sacrifice performed for several days and with great zeal and gaiety, the temple now had its annual 'kālotsava' (or brahmot-sava) spread over nine or ten days and conducted in splendour. The idea of five-fires (pañcāgni: sabhya, āhavanīya, anvāhārya, gārhapatya and āvasathya) was retained in the new conception of five iconic representations ("pañca-mūrti: Viṣṇu, Puruśa, Sayta, Acyuta and Aniruddha, and 'pañca-bera': dhruva, kautuka,
summary: This section contrasts Vedic sacrificial rituals (yajña) with temple-based iconic worship (pratimārādhana). It argues that iconic worship is superior because its benefits are permanent and universal, unlike the temporary and limited rewards of sacrifices. The text then demonstrates how the Vaikhānasa school systematically transformed the sacrificial cult into the cult of iconic worship by establishing direct correspondences. For example, the three sacrificial fires (tretāgni) correspond to the three main types of temple icons (bimba-traya), and specific Vedic rites like Soma-yāga were re-envisioned as annual temple festivals (brahmotsava).
key_themes: Transition from Vedic sacrifice to Agamic iconic worship
Theological justification for the superiority of iconic worship
Continuity and transformation in Hindu ritual practice
Systematization of iconic worship by the Vaikhānasa school
main_arguments: Iconic worship provides eternal and universally accessible benefits (acchinnaṃ śāśvataṃ nityaṃ), whereas the benefits of sacrificial rituals are temporary and confined to the performer (amūrtaṃ yajamānasya hyabhāve ca vinaśyati).
Iconic worship is all-encompassing, capable of fulfilling all desires (sarva-kāma-prada) and granting the fruits of all sacrifices (sarva-kratuphala-prada).

The Vaikhānasa tradition created a direct correspondence between the sacrificial fire-triad (tretāgni) and the temple's icon-triad (bimba-traya), thereby integrating and legitimizing iconic worship within a Vedic framework.
Temple culture did not simply replace the sacrificial cult but absorbed and reinterpreted it, with daily and occasional temple rituals becoming the new versions of older Vedic rites.
methodology: The methodology is primarily textual analysis and historical-comparative. The author cites and translates passages from Sanskrit texts (Yajñādhikāra and Prakīrṇādhikāra of the Vaikhānasa tradition) to support the central thesis. This textual evidence is then used to construct a historical argument about the evolution of religious practice from the Vedic sacrificial cult to the temple-centric iconic worship, highlighting a process of theological and ritual transformation rather than a complete rupture.
historiographical_context: The excerpt situates itself within the broader historical study of Hinduism, specifically addressing the pivotal shift from the Vedic period, characterized by aniconic fire sacrifices (yajña), to the later Puranic and Agamic periods, dominated by temple construction and idol worship (pūjā). By focusing on the Vaikhānasa school, the author argues for a model of continuity and systematic integration, challenging narratives that might portray this transition as a sharp break or a simple replacement. The argument frames the Vaikhānasa Āgamas as a crucial intellectual and ritual bridge between these two major phases of Hindu religious history.
research_questions: What were the theological arguments used to establish the superiority of permanent iconic worship over temporary sacrificial rituals?
How did the Vaikhānasa tradition systematically map the concepts and structures of the Vedic sacrificial cult onto the new practices of temple worship?

In what specific ways were key elements of Vedic ritual, such as the different types of sacred fires and annual sacrifices, transformed into corresponding elements of temple ritual, such as different types of icons and festivals?
What does this transformation reveal about the processes of continuity and change within the development of Hindu religious practice?
book_structure_overview: This excerpt functions as an introduction to a major theme of the book. The phrase, 'I will have occasion later to point out that...', indicates that the initial comparison and the role of the Vaikhānasa texts are foundational concepts. The subsequent chapters will likely delve deeper into these correspondences, providing more detailed analysis of the Vaikhānasa texts and other Āgamas to fully flesh out the argument that iconic worship is a structured evolution of the Vedic sacrificial cult.
